extracted.intended_audience: bankers, merchants, policymakers, and students of political economy
extracted.subtask_description: Principles and prudential criteria for bank behaviour concerning issuance of paper money, reserve management, discounting of bills, lending practices, and the risks of 'drawing and redrawing' (raising money by circulation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit of paper money that can circulate
rubrics_metrics.description: The whole paper money of every kind which can easily circulate in any country, never can exceed the value of the gold and silver, of which it supplies the place.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If circulating paper exceeds the specie that would otherwise be necessary (e.g., lowest note denomination threshold), the excess cannot be sent abroad or employed domestically and will return upon the banks to be exchanged for gold and silver. This creates runs as people demand payment from banks and the alarm amplifies the run.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reserve requirement when issuance exceeds circulation
rubrics_metrics.description: A banking company which issues more paper than can be employed in the circulation of the country... ought to increase the quantity of gold and silver which they keep at all times in their coffers, not only in proportion to this excessive increase of their circulation, but in a much greater proportion; their notes returning upon them much faster than in proportion to the excess of their quantity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: if a bank's absorbable circulation is £40,000 and it keeps £10,000 in specie for occasional demands, attempting to circulate £44,000 (an extra £4,000) would require increasing coffers to about £14,000 rather than only £11,000. The bank gains nothing from interest on the excessive paper and incurs continual expenses collecting and replacing specie which empties coffers faster.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two chief banking expenses to monitor
rubrics_metrics.description: The expenses peculiar to a bank consist chiefly in two articles: first, in the expense of keeping at all times in its coffers, for answering the occasional demands of the holders of its notes, a large sum of money, of which it loses the interest; and, secondly, in the expense of replenishing those coffers as fast as they are emptied by answering such occasional demands.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These two costs grow especially large when circulation is overstocked with paper: more specie must be held (loss of interest) and more frequent costly replenishment (collection, transport, insurance) is required; excessive circulation can make these expenses ruinous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid financing projects by drawing and redrawing ('raising money by circulation')
rubrics_metrics.description: The practice of drawing and redrawing... called raising money by circulation... This payment, therefore, was altogether fictitious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Drawing and redrawing involves successive short-dated bills drawn between parties and repeatedly discounted, accumulating interest and commissions (examples show effective costs often >8% and sometimes much higher). Though each bill is repaid in turn, the real value advanced by the original bill is never replaced to the banks. Such operations create fictitious capital, encourage over-trading, and often lead to bankruptcy when profits do not cover the enormous financing cost.

rubrics_metrics.name: Banks should only advance the part of capital equivalent to merchants' idle cash needs
rubrics_metrics.description: What a bank can with propriety advance to a merchant or undertaker of any kind, is not either the whole capital with which he trades... but that part of it only which he would otherwise be obliged to keep by him unemployed and in ready money, for answering occasional demands.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If advances never exceed this value they will not exceed the specie that would circulate absent paper money. Advances beyond this lead to excessive paper relative to what circulation can absorb and to species demands upon banks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discount only genuine bills of exchange drawn on real debtors
rubrics_metrics.description: When a bank discounts to a merchant a real bill of exchange, drawn by a real creditor upon a real debtor, and which, as soon as it becomes due, is really paid by that debtor; it only advances to him a part of the value which he would otherwise be obliged to keep by him unemployed and in ready money.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such discounting makes the bank's coffers resemble a water-pond where outflow is matched by inflow; little or no extraordinary expense is necessary to replenish coffers. Discounting genuine, self-liquidating paper is prudent banking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monitor short-period parity of advances and repayments
rubrics_metrics.description: The bank... ought to observe with great attention, whether, in the course of some short period (of four, five, six, or eight months, for example), the sum of the repayments which it commonly receives from them, is, or is not, fully equal to that of the advances which it commonly makes to them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If, within such short periods, repayments commonly equal advances, the bank may safely continue the relationship because inflows match outflows. If repayments commonly fall very much short of advances, continuing to deal with such customers is unsafe: outflows exceed inflows and coffers will be exhausted without extraordinary replenishment expense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Require frequent and regular operations from customers
rubrics_metrics.description: The banking companies of Scotland... were for a long time very careful to require frequent and regular repayments from all their customers, and did not care to deal with any person... who did not make, what they called, frequent and regular operations with them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Benefits: (1) allows banks to judge debtors' thriving or declining circumstances from their own books (regular vs irregular repayments) and (2) helps ensure the paper advanced does not exceed the quantity of specie the customer would otherwise have kept for occasional demands, preventing over-issuance of paper money.

rubrics_metrics.name: Banks should not fund fixed capital (long-term investments)
rubrics_metrics.description: Still less could a bank afford to advance him any considerable part of his fixed capital... The returns of the fixed capital are, in almost all cases, much slower than those of the circulating capital... such money ought not to be borrowed of a bank, but ought to be borrowed upon bond or mortgage, of such private people as propose to live upon the interest of their money.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fixed capital (e.g., forges, mines, land improvements) returns over years and is inappropriate for bank-style short-period advances; such long-term finance should come from lenders prepared to wait (mortgages, bonds), not deposit banks that require nearer-term repayment cycles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Excessive issuance forces costly coinage and export of specie
rubrics_metrics.description: By issuing too great a quantity of paper... the Bank of England was for many years together obliged to coin gold to the extent of between eight hundred thousand pounds and a million a-year... the bank... was frequently obliged to purchase gold bullion at the high price of four pounds an ounce, which it soon after issued in coin at £3:17:10½ an ounce, losing... upon the coinage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Excess paper returning on banks forces them to supply specie (coinage) to the kingdom; this may involve buying bullion at high prices, coining at a loss, having good coin melted down or exported, and yet still finding the domestic scarcity of good coin unchanged. The indirect costs and losses fall on banks (and indirectly on the public).
